newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli finance minister lauds budget passage.
newsitem.headline: Israeli finance minister lauds budget passage.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor on Wednesday expressed satisfaction with the government's 1997 budget, approved by parliament early this morning.
"We did it," he declared in English at a news conference.
"The budget cut approved this morning strengthens our economic standing in the world," he added.

Meridor said the cost of the compromises made with legislators needed to win approval of the budget amounted to 350 million shekels. He said the money would come out of the budget reserve, which is approximately 1.4 billion shekels.

Meridor would not say how he would fill a further 270 million shekel gap created by parliament's refusal to cancel a special half-point tax credit for working women. However, he hinted that he might raise taxes, saying he would take no more funds from the reserves and that finding additional spending cuts would be very difficult.

The Israeli government's 1997 budget of just under 190 billion shekels includes spending cuts, new taxes and other revenue measures totalling about seven billion shekels. The Treasury is seeking to keep this year's deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product.

Meridor warned that this year's budget "will finish off badly" because revenues in December were lower than expected. Revenues lagged behind forecasts all of 1996, causing the deficit to swell to an estimated four percent or more of GDP.

With the budget passed, Meridor said he now intended to turn immediately to other items on his policy agenda. He said he would re-submit to the cabinet shortly the recommendations of the Brodet panel on capital market reform as well as plans for structural reforms in the economy, particularly public transport.

In October, the cabinet refused to accept some of the key recommendations of the Brodet panel aimed at encouraging long-term saving. Its most controversial proposal was to impose taxes on short-term savings.
Meridor hinted that he expected the Bank of Israel to cut interest rates further now that the budget was approved.
"Monetary policy has to correspond to fiscal policy. Fiscal policy is now perfect," he said.
